channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 authentication bypass in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active exploitation — that box is the IT/OT boundary TSA asks you to prove
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active exploitation. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance operating system. Cisco fixed it in early March and published indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos tracks three clusters of post-compromise activity across this flaw and the earlier CVE-2026-20316: an unattributed cluster that used CVE-2026-20079 to plant a web shell and a JAR-based command executor and steal credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both flaws, whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm’s and which deployed a Cyclops Blink variant; and UAT-11988, a ransomware operator that got in only through the CVE-2026-20316 static credentials and ultimately deployed Qilin. CVE-2026-20316 has been in KEV since 29 July, flagged for known ransomware use. For railroads and transit agencies the consequence is specific. TSA security directives require a documented, tested separation between IT and critical cyber systems — dispatch, signalling support, traction-power SCADA, fare and station systems. FMC is where that separation is enforced, and root there lets an attacker edit it silently. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek; Talos cluster wording re-checked 16 Sep 2026 - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; re-checked 11 Sep 2026, no change of state

item.title: [Critical] FBI seizes the Chinese state-sponsored platforms that scanned US critical infrastructure and relayed the attacks through hijacked devices
item.category: Incident — State-sponsored reconnaissance infrastructure seized
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms run by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan performed reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed the resulting intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic arrived from ordinary domestic addresses. Both are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware for command and authentication. Named victims are federal, and the described activity runs back to at least 2018. For railroads and transit agencies the relay layer is the transferable point: a rail estate is full of small, internet-connected, unpatched devices — and the source address in your logs never proved anything. - US Department of Justice press release and unsealed court documents — corroborated by TechCrunch and UPI - Seizures announced and confirmed 26 Aug 2026; described activity dates from at least 2018 to 2026

item.title: [High] A suspected China-linked group stole SCADA and HMI source code from an automation vendor — the repositories were self-hosted, reachable and running an unpatched Gitea
item.category: Incident — State-linked theft of industrial engineering material
item.description: Acronis threat intelligence published findings on 13 September on an actor it calls Red Heron, which has been exploiting CVE-2026-60004, a critical remote code execution flaw in self-hosted Gitea, since 29 July 2026. The group scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and confirmed compromises at at least 11 organisations — Acronis counts 11 targets in five countries, while The Hacker News reports 13 organisations in six. Two victims matter here. A Taiwanese industrial-automation company lost repositories covering SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-sniffer products. A Canadian renewable-energy firm lost infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens. The toolset includes the JITTERLY Linux implant, a new self-restoring LD_PRELOAD rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT, and the Adaptix C2 framework. Attribution to a Chinese-speaking group is moderate confidence, resting on language artefacts and tradecraft; the compromises themselves are confirmed. No rail organisation is among the named victims, but the exposure class is one transit owns outright: signalling, SCADA and passenger-information work is contracted out, and the contractor’s repository server holds the project files, controller logic and credentials for your estate. - Acronis threat intelligence — reported by Industrial Cyber and The Hacker News - Acronis report 13 Sep 2026; exploitation traced back to 29 Jul 2026; KEV-listed 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Transport and logistics organisations are part of the surge. For rail and transit the exposure is rarely the signalling system itself — it is dispatch support, crew management, maintenance planning, fare collection and passenger information, all of which can degrade service without any train control being touched. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. Rail has practised this for a century without calling it cybersecurity: interlocking, fail-safe signalling and vital logic exist precisely so that a failure upstream cannot produce an unsafe movement. The current argument is that those principles should be applied deliberately to digital systems rather than assumed to still hold. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] An entire credential campaign, start to finish, in under six hours — Google documents autonomous agents doing the work
item.category: Threat Intel — Autonomous multi-agent intrusion tooling
item.description: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated group completed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework, with the agents rather than human operators carrying it through. GTIG separately observed actors stealing AI API credentials and running unauthorised workloads inside victims’ own cloud tenants across healthcare, government and media. Its guidance is to assume every actor is now using AI to some degree. The rail consequence is arithmetic, not novelty. Credential phishing against dispatchers, crew callers, maintenance planners and contractor accounts is the standard opening move, and a campaign that completes inside six hours finishes well before a Monday-morning review — and comfortably inside the overnight window when the operations control centre is staffed but the security team is not. - Google Threat Intelligence Group reporting — via The Hacker News - Published 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
item.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident
item.description: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a railroad or transit operator the implication is the escalation path: signalling, dispatch and traction-power systems sit behind corporate networks monitored on a business-hours rhythm an autonomous attacker does not share. - Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index and the report “The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker”, reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor-published research; the figures are the authors’ own test results and have not been independently reproduced - Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six steps to being able to disconnect — and a planning horizon of three months in degraded mode
item.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
item.description: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. Rail already understands graduated degradation better than most sectors — degraded-mode working is a rehearsed discipline, not a novelty. What CI Fortify adds is the requirement to pre-build the separation points rather than improvise them, and to keep monitoring alive on the isolated side. Nozomi’s planning horizon of up to three months is the uncomfortable part: most rail degraded-mode procedures assume hours or days of manual working, not a quarter. - Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance - Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] Researchers used an AI model to port a working PLC exploit to a sibling controller — then bricked one
item.category: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For rail and transit the relevant detail is fleet uniformity in reverse: wayside, station and depot control estates are assembled from close variants of the same controller families, and an exploit proven on one variant is now materially cheaper to move onto its siblings. - Forescout Vedere Labs research reported by SecurityWeek - Reported 1 Sep 2026; underlying flaw CVE-2021-31886 disclosed 2021

item.title: [Critical] NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting
item.description: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. It names no victims, actors or techniques. Rail is not called out, but the exposure pattern the NCSC describes is the one railways carry structurally: assets spread across hundreds of miles, reached over carrier links, commissioned by integrators, and running long-lived equipment nobody replaces on an IT cycle. The alert’s core instruction — do not assume your OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure comes from misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets — applies directly to level-crossing controllers, wayside cabinets, SCADA for traction power and tunnel ventilation, depot and yard systems, and station building management. It also aligns closely with what TSA security directives already require of US passenger and freight carriers. - UK National Cyber Security Centre alert, “Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices” - Published 27 Aug 2026; the NCSC says it has been engaging affected sectors directly ahead of publication

item.title: [Critical] CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
item.category: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings
item.description: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes paired red-team results from two critical-infrastructure organisations assessed with comparable tradecraft. One detected and responded; the other never noticed a domain compromise. The advisory is direct that the difference was not product spend — both had capable tooling, but only one reviewed the output, correlated identity events and had practised the response. Transit agencies and railroads recognise the pattern because dispatch, maintenance, fare collection and corporate systems so often share one Active Directory, and because operational networks are frequently left outside monitoring on the grounds that the alerts would be too noisy to action. - CISA advisory AA26-237A — corroborated by CyberScoop and The Hacker News - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] ConnectWise ScreenConnect joins KEV with attackers already pushing scripts to endpoints as they connect — the second remote-support console in five days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, remote support
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 September. It is a missing-authorisation flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, scored CVSS 9.9, that permits unauthorised file transfer and code execution, and three separate incidents are documented in which threat actors abused it to push malicious scripts to endpoints at the moment those endpoints connected. A patch is available and the federal remediation deadline was 14 September. Arriving five days after N-able N-central landed in the same catalogue at CVSS 10.0, this is the same failure twice inside a week, in the two consoles third parties most often use to reach industrial estates. ScreenConnect in particular travels in the field-service bag: signalling contractors, fare-collection vendors, SCADA integrators and building-systems suppliers install it to support what they commissioned, frequently without a change record, and frequently on machines that also talk to the operational network. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 11 Sep 2026, with the ConnectWise advisory — reported by The Hacker News - Added to KEV 11 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and rail and transit teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Passenger and freight operators keep dispatch, CAD/AVL, passenger-information, fare-collection and back-office signalling support code in self-hosted GitLab instances that often sit on the corporate side with routed paths into the operational network. Unauthenticated file reads expose the credentials and integration detail that bridge those two worlds. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA flags a CVSS 9.8 missing-authorisation flaw in mySCADA myPRO Manager — and lists Transportation among the sectors running it
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA/HMI management, unexploited
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-258-03 on 15 September covering mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. It carries two flaws: CVE-2026-73807, a missing-authorisation vulnerability scored CVSS v3 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567, missing authentication for a critical function, scored 6.3. Together they could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a GSM modem connected to the system. mySCADA has fixed both in version 2.2. CISA lists the deployed sectors as Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Food and Agriculture, Transportation and Water, and states that no known public exploitation targeting these flaws has been reported to it. No rail or transit deployment is named in the advisory. The relevance here is inventory: small SCADA and HMI packages turn up in station plant, pumping, tunnel ventilation and depot systems commissioned by integrators, and an SMS-capable modem on such a system is often the alarm path to on-call staff. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03 - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Four PROFINET DCP flaws in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 edge gateway — mostly patched, unexploited, and worth an inventory check
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch, vulnerability research
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs disclosed four memory-corruption vulnerabilities in the PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol implementation on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 industrial PC in a 10 September write-up, reported by Industrial Cyber on 15 September. Tracked as CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578, each carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 5.3 and affects firmware up to V4.0 HF0. The set comprises an uninitialised-value flaw, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads. The flawed DCP daemon runs as root, requires no authentication and is bound to all three device interfaces, so an attacker with access to the same Layer 2 segment can crash it with crafted Ethernet frames — making the device appear unreachable to SCADA, or preventing it from obtaining an IP address during commissioning. The flaws are covered by Siemens advisory SSA-327438, first published in May 2025, so this is new research on known CVEs rather than a new advisory; version 1.1 of that advisory lists no fix for CVE-2025-40578. There is no reported exploitation. Rail and transit estates that use the LPE9403 as an edge processing node in depots, traction power rooms or station plant rooms should note that the flawed service runs as root, unauthenticated, on every device interface. The realistic outcome is loss of view of the device rather than loss of control of the process. - Nozomi Networks Labs research and Siemens ProductCERT SSA-327438 — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Nozomi research 10 Sep 2026; Industrial Cyber reporting 15 Sep 2026; Siemens SSA-327438 first published May 2025

item.title: [Critical] N-able N-central lands in KEV at CVSS 10 — the console many transit and short-line IT providers run
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September. The lead item is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code injection flaw scored CVSS 10.0 that yields pre-authentication remote code execution. N-able confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal remediation deadline was 11 September and has now passed. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform: an agent with system-level rights on every managed endpoint, operated by a third party. Short lines, commuter authorities and municipal transit agencies commonly outsource back-office IT to providers running exactly this console. Also added were two Windows zero-days granting SYSTEM and an Adobe Commerce injection flaw. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026, with N-able and Huntress reporting — corroborated by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; vendor hotfix released 5 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] NetScaler and FortiOS are confirmed exploited and in KEV — the two boxes most often standing between a supplier and a rail OT network
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, network edge
item.description: CISA added two more edge products to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 9 September. The first is an authentication bypass in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, CVE-2026-19490 at CVSS 9.3, affecting AAA virtual server and Gateway configurations; honeypot telemetry recorded 56 exploitation attempts from 3 September, 36 of them on 8 September alone. The second is a heap buffer overflow in Fortinet FortiOS, FortiSwitchManager and FortiSASE, CVE-2025-25249 at CVSS 7.3, exploited since July 2026 in a campaign distributing the PivotC2 remote access trojan that has reached more than 3,000 addresses, with an estimated 178 FortiGate devices found infected and the concentration in the United States. Both carried a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. This supersedes the August NetScaler item previously carried here. Neither of these is an IT asset in any useful sense for a railroad: the NetScaler gateway is how the signalling supplier gets in, and the FortiGate is often the only device between the corporate network and a dispatch or SCADA segment. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue additions of 9 Sep 2026, with Citrix and Fortinet advisories — reported by The Hacker News - Added to KEV 9 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 12 Sep 2026; FortiOS exploitation traced to July 2026

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska confirms the MikroTik “MikroTrick” chain is now being exploited — the router class that quietly backhauls remote rail sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Edge routers, confirmed exploited in the wild
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerability chain known as “MikroTrick”, previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited, is now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication-bypass flaw, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device. A third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, describing only the exposure category: MikroTik devices are widely deployed by internet service providers, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. Nothing in the alert ties the activity to rail or transit. The relevance for this audience is inventory rather than attribution — low-cost RouterOS hardware is a common choice for backhaul at remote, unstaffed sites such as crossings, wayside cabinets, yard offices and small stations, and a router compromised at that layer sits upstream of whatever segmentation you rely on. - CERT Polska alert of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by Industrial Cyber; no victim, sector or critical-infrastructure impact named in the source - Exploitation confirmed 9 Sep 2026; activity observed since at least 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September’s ICS patch round lands on Modicon controllers, RTUs and the protection relays behind traction power
item.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday, controllers and protection relays
item.description: Schneider Electric published four advisories on 8 September, the most severe a critical authentication vulnerability in the Modicon M580 and Modicon M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2. Also fixed: high-severity flaws in the PowerLogic T300 RTU — formerly the Easergy T300, a distribution-automation RTU that turns up in traction-power and substation retrofits — and in EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, plus a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven on 8 September, headlined by ProductCERT SSA-142885: fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays for all versions before V2.70, led by CVE-2026-62645 (CVSS v3.1 9.8), where the web interface leaks enough data to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication. Siemens also patched Industrial Edge Management and Open Interface Services, and Aveva fixed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, which CISA published on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: a hardcoded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-81821) and a weak password-hashing algorithm (CVE-2026-81822), both CVSS v3 8.4, plus a missing-authorisation flaw (CVE-2026-81823, 5.3) and a cross-site scripting flaw (CVE-2026-81824, 4.7), all fixed in 2025 SP1 P2. That product is an oil-and-gas pipeline leak-detection tool rather than a rail one, and is listed here for completeness of the September round. CISA republished the Reyrolle 7SR5 advisory as ICSA-26-258-05 and the SCADAPack x70 advisory as ICSA-26-258-04 on 15 September. No exploitation is reported for any of it. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-142885 and the September Schneider Electric and Aveva security advisories — round-up via SecurityWeek - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 covering the Aveva flaws published 10 Sep 2026; Reyrolle 7SR5 and SCADAPack x70 republished by CISA 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch targets the remote-access client and the firmware updater — IXON, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform
item.description: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September, and three land on the remote-support path that rail and transit operators rely on. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client: CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7. Wayside cabinets, depot systems and station plant are routinely supported through exactly this kind of managed VPN client. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 lets commands or code run at the logged-in user’s permission level — ControlFLASH is how firmware reaches the controllers behind platform-edge doors, yard equipment and depot machinery. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects. None is reported as exploited. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-02 (IXON VPN Client), ICSA-26-246-03 (Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH) and ICSA-26-246-06 (Inductive Automation Ignition) - Published 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos - Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September ICS batch is mostly Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patch available
item.description: CISA published eight industrial control system advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The one most sites will notice first is ICSA-26-244-01, covering four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625. All four are remotely triggerable with no authentication and no user interaction: a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet crashes the RSLinx Classic service. Rockwell has fixed all four in version 4.60. The rest of the batch covers the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (ICSA-26-244-02), the Logix platform (-03, reaching ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). No exploitation has been reported for any of them. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through ICSA-26-244-05, published 1 Sep 2026, cross-checked against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index - Advisories published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
item.category: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue
item.description: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch that included NetScaler. None is a rail product, and that is the relevant point for a sector whose safety systems are usually well separated but whose operations are not. CVE-2026-53362 is a Linux kernel flaw, and the traffic management server, passenger information system, CCTV recorder, network sensor and many wayside gateways are Linux underneath — often vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s schedule rather than the operator’s. CVE-2026-66384 is a path traversal in JFrog Artifactory, relevant wherever firmware and software builds bound for onboard or wayside equipment are staged. CVE-2023-49105 is an ownCloud authentication bypass patched since late 2023; the instances still exposed tend to be ones no team owns. Wabtec’s data leak this month is a reminder that rail’s IT layer is already being worked. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition, corroborated by Security Affairs and SecurityWeek - Added to KEV 27 Aug 2026; ownCloud flaw originally disclosed Nov 2023

item.title: [High] CISA advisory on a heavy-vehicle brake controller — exploitation costs ABS, traction control and the speedometer
item.category: Advisory — Commercial vehicle braking ECU, safety functions
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-237-05 on 25 August covering the Bendix EC80 brake electronic control unit, used in heavy commercial vehicles. According to the advisory, successful exploitation could cause loss of anti-lock braking functions, steering assist, the speedometer and shifting capability, or disable automatic traction control. This lands on the rail and transit page because most transit agencies are also bus operators, and the same vehicle-network exposure applies to the non-revenue and maintenance fleet that supports rail operations. Foundation braking is unaffected — the failure modes described are the electronic assistance layered on top of it — but a bus losing ABS and traction control in service is a safety event, not a maintenance one. Mitigation is a vehicle-network access and firmware question rather than a patch you apply centrally. - CISA advisory ICSA-26-237-05, Bendix EC80 Brake ECU - Advisory published 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Rail operators are largely beneficiaries rather than regulated parties, but rolling-stock, signalling and passenger-system suppliers selling into the EU now carry the reporting duty, and their disclosure timelines should tighten accordingly. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Info] TSA reopens its surface-transportation cyber information collection — and the vetting rule for coordinators has changed
item.category: Regulation & Policy — TSA surface transportation, comments due 1 Oct 2026
item.description: TSA published a Federal Register notice on 1 September covering the revised information collection for higher-risk freight rail, mass transit and passenger rail, and over-the-road bus owners and operators, with comments due 1 October 2026. The collection carries forward the substance of the security directives rather than replacing it: designated primary and alternate cybersecurity coordinators, 72-hour incident reporting to CISA, a Cybersecurity Incident Response Plan, and Cybersecurity Implementation and Assessment Plans with annual assessment reports. One change is worth flagging to HR and legal now — introduced in the 15 January 2026 revision of SD 1580-21-01 and SD 1582-21-01, a cybersecurity coordinator who is not a US citizen must hold NEXUS, Global Entry or equivalent TSA-approved vetting. TSA also re-estimated the burden at 67 respondents and 22,167 hours, down from 846 and 210,684. - TSA notice, “Revision of Agency Information Collection Activity Under OMB Review: Cybersecurity Measures for Surface Modes” — via the Federal Register - Published 1 Sep 2026; comments due 1 Oct 2026; underlying SD 1580-21-01 and SD 1582-21-01 revised 15 Jan 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal incident-reporting rules across 27 agencies — and a transit agency can sit inside several clocks at once
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Incident reporting burden
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, citing GAO work, counting 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which reach private industry. The argument is operational rather than political: filings with different thresholds, formats and deadlines pull the same small group of people away from containment during the hours that matter most. Rail sits in an unusually crowded corner of that map. A single event at a transit authority can trigger the 72-hour report to CISA required under the TSA security directives, an FTA or state safety oversight notification, a local emergency-management report, a breach notification if rider or payment data is involved, and — once CIRCIA rules are finalised, expected this autumn — a further CISA filing on its own clock. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO findings — via Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026

item.title: [Medium] The free assessment small operators actually used is being withdrawn — and nothing at that price replaces it
item.category: Policy — CISA reported to be ending six free critical-infrastructure assessment services
item.description: Cybersecurity Dive reported on 3 September that CISA has told staff to stop delivering six of the free assessment services it has offered critical-infrastructure owners, including its on-site architecture design review and several facilitated risk and resilience assessments, following an internal direction reportedly given on 25 August. The agency had not published a formal notice as of this edition, so the exact scope and end dates should be read as reported rather than confirmed. For rail the exposure is at the smaller end: short lines, regional freight operators and municipal transit agencies that fall under the TSA directives but have no in-house assessment capability and no budget line for a commercial equivalent. - Cybersecurity Dive reporting, carried by Utility Dive — based on an internal CISA meeting described by people familiar with it; no formal agency notice had been published as of this edition - Direction reportedly given 25 Aug 2026; reported 3 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance for IT and OT service providers — and a transit operator is one
item.category: Policy — Joint international guidance, incident communications
item.description: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It asks for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates rather than legal boilerplate, root-cause and technical detail that end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory duties. Rail and transit sit on both sides of this. You are a consumer of it when a signalling, ticketing or fleet-telematics supplier goes dark, and you are the provider when a degraded-mode day has to be explained to passengers, freight customers and a regulator at the same time. - Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and CISA — joint guidance “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers” - Published 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Britain moves to bar designated high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure — without naming them publicly
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Proposed, not yet in force
item.description: The UK government has tabled late amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let ministers stop critical-sector organisations from using technology suppliers designated as high risk. The Bill, introduced in November 2025 and now near the end of its passage through the Lords, already extends duties to energy, water, transport and health operators and pulls managed service providers, data centres and digital infrastructure into scope. The amendments were tabled on 24 August and reported on 2 September; they follow reporting that a small UK generating station ran manually for four days after a cyberattack. Designations would not necessarily be made public, which is the detail operators should notice: a supplier could be designated without a public list to check against, so the obligation to know your own supply chain moves from good practice to compliance exposure. None of this is in force yet, and the Bill has not completed its passage. - SecurityWeek reporting on the amendments tabled to the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill - Amendments tabled 24 Aug 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; not yet in force — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
item.category: Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligation
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware, with fuller reporting to follow. Railways sit on both sides of this. Operators buying rolling stock, signalling and station systems from European suppliers gain a defined notification obligation to write into contracts; operators or subsidiaries that themselves place connected products on the EU market acquire the obligation directly. - EU Regulation 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) and European Commission implementation guidance - Obligations apply from 11 Sep 2026; phase-start reporting reviewed 1 Sep 2026; re-verified 4 Sep 2026
